Hello. I've been trying to create a transmission hologram using a single beam setup (half strikes object and half on the plate) but I cant seem to make my holograms brighter. I guess my problem is on correct beam ratio. Is there a way to compensate for this? (like different developing techniques?)

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
There is a messy solution, however it is cheap. Get a piece of gray gel from a theater or anything that can attenuate the light. Like a partially silvered mirror any smoked glass be creative. Place this in the beam on the reference half. 

Here is the messy part, the edge of the attenuator will cause all sorts of beam quality problems down stream, so you need to make sure these go in between the plate and the object.

I had a little attenuator I had used made from a Neutral Density Gel from a local theater glued to a piece of thin glass salvaged from a picture frame. If I had to make another one I think I would ditch the glass and try to make a "stretcher" for the gel as the edge effect was always a problem.

A red gel would work as well, I just had my choice and ND gels are more intuitive for 4th graders to understand. If you give it a try please post your results as I am working on a section for the wiki on single beam work. (Photos always take me for ever )

posts.author: javamiggs
posts.content_md:
I have one flat front-surfaced mirror (4x6 inches) but I really wanted to use just a single beam.

Here's what I did.

I used a photometer that could measure relative intensities and I calibrated the meter on the reference beam. I covered the object beam and placed the meter probe behind the plate (used plate) and set the photometer on 100% illuminance using ref beam. Then I covered the reference and let the meter read reflected light from the object again from behind the plate. I could not get a constant reading but at some areas of the plate, more or less the object beam is 20%-30% less intense than the reference beam. Now if I take 25% as my mean, I could have a beam ratio of roughly 4:1(ref:obj). I achieved this by optimizing the geometry of my set-up (done by many trial and error) and spray-painted my object very very white. But this ratio is not for the whole area of the plate. The illuminance of my diode laser decreases at the edges. I haven't yet tried to shoot a hologram in this set-up since I have one more doubt in my mind. Is it a requirement that the beam ratio should be constant throughout the area of the plate?

Also, I learned that:

"beam ratio depends on the "bandwidth" of the data. The bandwidth is determined by the range of angles formed between the object beam and the reference beam."

I wonder what these "range of angles" are.

When I optimized my geometry, I carefully considered that the angle between ref and obj beams does not exceed 70 degrees. I calculated this angle from the resolving power of my emulsion (PFG-01) and the wavelength of my laser (670nm).

posts.author: javamiggs
posts.content_md: Basically what I did was working backwards. Since I could not alter my reference beam, I looked for ways and means to make my object beam atleast 25% less intense than the reference beam measured at the plate.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: JohnFP, how are the systems you described above "single beam" systems? Spatial beamsplitting is still beamsplitting. Perhaps a better description would be "single beam expander". As you add complexity, the addition of another simple, cheap beam expanding optic will certainly give better control of the beams and results.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Well Bob that is an interesting point. What exactly is a single beam. 

In my two configurations there is no single optic that allows the beam to pass through and reflect off off it at the same time thus not a split beam set up because there is no single optic that splits the beam. This may be trivial but without a thick piece of glass or an expensive "beam splitter" there will be unwanted reflections off that optic. As my systems use mirrors only to devide the beam there is no such problem.

Then I have to ask, if one does a single beam tranmisison but addes a mirror to catch overflow light and redirect it to the object for additional lighting is that a single beam? I believe the technique of steeling light and redirecting it to the object is referred to in a few publications and they call it a single beam

Also, is a standard single beam (SBR or SBT) really a single beam. I mean, no matter which type of hologram you make you need two beams, a reference and an object beam. There are no hologram that actually use a single beam or there would be no interference. It all depends where and how you split it, even if it is at the object, optic etc...

So my logic may be wrong but again I was under the assumption that a single beam is one in which there is no single optic that actually splits (allows part to pass through and part to reflect) the beam.

But I am surely open for persuasion.

posts.author: Tony
posts.content_md:
Even though you don't have a beam splitter per se, this is really a split beam transmission setup. The stability requirements are more stringent than for a single beam reflection where the object and the plate can be locked together. I suspect object motion may be an issue.

Also, even though your object appears bright, it may be affecting the polarization of the reflected light in a way that reduces brightness. Try rotating the laser to change the polarization, and/or view the setup through a polarized filter (sunglasses) to see if the polarization is being affected.

It is possible to make a hologram that is brighter than the original object. This is mentioned in Steve Benton's lectures on holography:

[http://splweb.bwh.harvard.edu:8000/cour ... _Holos.pdf](http://splweb.bwh.harvard.edu:8000/courses/mas450/reading/chaptersPDF/Ch07_Platonic_Holos.pdf)

...on page 6 right after equation 18.

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md:
Saxby in the new "Practical Holography" edition refers to setups using spatially split beams, especially where a neutral density filter is used to reduce the reference beam brightness, as "bypass" setups, a term which I recommend.

Usually objects are not nearly as bright as we would want, so reducing the reference beam brightness helps to get the reference/object beam ratio closer to the ideal value which resuts in brighter holograms at the expense of a longer required exposure time. 

The ideal ratio depends on many things, but is usually supposed to be higher for transmission holograms than for reflection holos. Ranges for ideal reference:object beam ratios found in a quick check of a few handbooks range from 10:1 to 3:1 for transmission holos versus 4:1 to 2:1 for reflection holos.
